title: Most people remember the cross.
paragraphs: Most people remember the cross.
Few remember the man who gave Jesus a tomb.
His name was Joseph of Arimathea.

He was not one of the famous disciples.
He did not preach sermons like Peter.
He did not write letters like Paul.
He did not walk on water or feed thousands.
Yet in one quiet moment of courage, Joseph did something that forever placed his name inside the story of the resurrection.
He gave Jesus his tomb.
But to understand how powerful this was, you have to understand the moment in which it happened.
Jesus had just been crucified.

The crowds that once shouted “Hosanna” had gone silent.
Rome had executed Him like a criminal.
The religious leaders believed the threat was over.
To the world, Jesus looked defeated.
Hope seemed buried before the burial even began.
Many of the disciples were hiding in fear.
But Joseph stepped forward.
The Gospel of Mark says something remarkable:
“Joseph of Arimathea… went boldly to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body.” (Mark 15:43)
Boldly.
That word matters.

Joseph was not just an ordinary citizen.
Scripture tells us he was a respected member of the council — the same governing body that had condemned Jesus.
To publicly associate himself with Jesus at that moment could damage his reputation, his influence, and possibly his safety.
But grief and devotion overcame fear.
Joseph went directly to Pilate and asked for the body of the crucified Messiah.
And then he did something even more costly.
He offered his own tomb.
Matthew tells us it was a new tomb that Joseph himself had cut out of the rock (Matthew 27:60).
This was not a random grave.

In ancient Jewish culture, tombs were expensive and carefully prepared.
They were family burial places, symbols of honor, dignity, and legacy.
Joseph had prepared that tomb for himself.
Yet when Jesus needed a place to be buried, Joseph surrendered what he had reserved for his own future.
Think about the weight of that moment.

While others distanced themselves from Jesus,
Joseph moved closer.

While others protected their reputation,
Joseph risked his.

While others waited to see what would happen,
Joseph acted.
Real devotion often reveals itself in moments like this.
Not when faith is celebrated.
But when faith becomes costly.
Anyone can follow Jesus when the crowd is cheering.
Anyone can praise Him when blessings are visible.
But the question of true devotion often appears in quieter moments:
When following Christ could cost something.
Joseph’s decision reminds us of something powerful.
Sometimes the most meaningful acts of faith are not loud.
They are sacrificial.
Joseph did not preach a sermon.
He prepared a resting place.
He did not stand before a crowd.
He honored Jesus in a moment of sorrow.
And yet that act became part of the greatest miracle in history.
Because the tomb Joseph gave…
became the tomb that could not hold Christ.
The place of burial became the place where resurrection would soon be declared.
What Joseph surrendered became part of the testimony of victory.
This is one of the quiet mysteries of faith.
When we place something in Jesus’ hands, it is never wasted.
Joseph thought he was giving up a tomb.
In reality, he was participating in a moment that billions of people would remember forever.
His act of honor became part of the story of resurrection morning.
And that raises an important question for us today.
What are we holding onto that God may be asking us to surrender?
Sometimes we think discipleship is only about belief.
But Scripture often shows that devotion reveals itself through sacrifice.
Not everyone is asked to give the same thing.
For some people it is comfort.
For others it is pride.
For some it is reputation.
For others it is control over their own plans.
Joseph reminds us that following Jesus sometimes means making room for Him where we once reserved space for ourselves.
And here is the beautiful irony.
The tomb Joseph gave Jesus did not remain occupied.
Three days later…
it was empty.
The place Joseph surrendered became a witness to the greatest victory in human history.
Death was defeated.
Hope was restored.
The stone was rolled away.
And the man Joseph buried was no longer there.
Because Jesus had risen.
Sometimes what we surrender to God becomes part of a story far bigger than we imagined.
Joseph of Arimathea may not have been the loudest disciple.
But in one moment of courage, he showed the world what costly devotion looks like.
He gave Jesus what he had prepared for himself.
And that simple act reminds us of a timeless truth:
Real love for Christ is often revealed by what we are willing to place in His hands.

Scripture:
Matthew 27:57–60
Mark 15:43
Luke 23:50–53
John 19:38–42
If this message spoke to you, reflect on this:
What is one thing in your life that you may need to surrender to make more room for Jesus?
